extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (researchers and graduate students) preparing proofs or self-reviewing work before publication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors to judge the reliability of their own proofs by listing warning signs of likely errors and describing features of genuine problem-solving. A checklist to use before claiming a result or submitting for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspect effortless solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you unexpectedly find a problem solving itself almost effortlessly, and you can't quite see why, you should try to analyse your solution more sceptically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unusually smooth solution is a red flag: re-examine each step, seek hidden assumptions, and attempt to re-derive the result by alternative means to ensure the ease is genuine rather than due to a subtle mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test method strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether your approach can prove statements known to be false — this reveals methodological flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately apply your method to false or borderline statements; if it 'proves' them, the method likely lacks necessary restrictions or contains a logical gap. Use such stress-tests to identify where hypotheses are being smuggled in or where arguments are too permissive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek counterexamples first
rubrics_metrics.description: Before proving ambitious claims, hunt for counterexamples; either you'll save time or gain insight into necessary proof conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively look for small or toy counterexamples before investing in a full proof. Finding a counterexample saves wasted effort; failing to find one can reveal the precise extra hypotheses you need or guide you to correct formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flag: sudden simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: When difficulty drops suddenly mid-proof, scrutinise that transition; it likely contains the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a hard argument suddenly becomes trivial, inspect the step where complexity collapses for hidden use of stronger assumptions, unjustified cancellations, or covert case-splitting. Reproduce the transition in detail and try to construct edge cases that break it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine proof-by-contradiction integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether your reductio works without your initial assumption — if so, the assumption wasn't essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the contradiction truly depends on the negated hypothesis. Try running the argument without that hypothesis: if the contradiction still follows, you may have accidentally proved an unattainable implication or used circular reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for topic drift
rubrics_metrics.description: Be suspicious if computations move far from the problem's core mathematical context and connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your calculations or constructions increasingly rely on machinery or domains unrelated to the original problem, pause and reassess relevance. Topic drift can indicate you're proving something different (or weaker/stronger) than intended, or that essential hypotheses have been introduced tacitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question 'novel twists'
rubrics_metrics.description: When adapting established methods with your unique modification that experts 'missed,' expect hidden technical flaws others avoided deliberately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ingenious-seeming small modifications with skepticism: check why standard methods failed and why your tweak should fix that; hunt for the technical obstacles experts avoided, and validate your twist across representative examples and boundary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of genuine problem-solving (plausibility check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine problem-solving usually involves incremental progress on toy models, method refinement, discovering limitations, integrating insights from other fields, and iterative development over years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence or absence of these patterns as a plausibility test: if your 'solution' lacks incremental toy-model testing, visible refinement, or evidence of grappling with limitations, treat it as more likely to be flawed. Conversely, documented iterative development and cross-checks increase confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good proof passes self-skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' proof passes self-skepticism: the author has actively tried to break their own argument and failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before declaring a result, actively attempt to refute it (search for counterexamples, stress-test methods, examine simplifications, etc.). Passing these deliberate attacks is a practical standard for readiness to publish or present a proof.
